But Hazara was initially part of the transfer to Gulab Singh and only in early 1847 did he cede it back to the Lahore Darbar, so 1846 is without Hazara (Cliopatria's 1848 shape); the ledger returns it in 1847.

correction.text: the Lahore state with Hazara, back under the Darbar since early 1847

correction.text: the Lahore state with Hazara, until the annexation of the Punjab by the East India Company

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe: Cliopatria's last shape is 1848, but the Empire lasted to the proclamation of 29 March 1849 (annexation formally 2 April). Same shape as 1848 as corrected.

ledger.note: 7 July 1799: Ranjit Singh captures Lahore. Infobox 'Capture of Lahore by Ranjit Singh: 7 July 1799'; the lead: 'It existed from 1799, when maharaja Ranjit Singh captured Lahore, to 1849'. He was crowned on 12 April 1801. The page does not say from whom Lahore was taken; it lay inside Cliopatria's Sikh Confederacy shape of 1799.

ledger.counterpart: Jammu (the ruler of the Jammu region)
ledger.note: 1800: Jammu comes under Ranjit Singh. 'In 1800, the Jammu region was annexed by Ranjit Singh' (Ranjit Singh page: 'the ruler of the Jammu region ceded control of his region to Ranjit Singh'). 'Ranjit Singh had restored Gulab Singh Dogra the estates of his father at Jammu in 1820 as jagir.' No Cliopatria shape holds Jammu before 1820.

region.text: the central Punjab between the Jhelum and the Sutlej in Cliopatria's 1800 shape

ledger.note: 1800: the Punjab core. Cliopatria's shape jumps from Lahore (2,700 km2) to 57,500 km2 in 1800; the pages opened give no year for these lands (they have the misls absorbed from 1802 to 1813). Confidence 1: the year is Cliopatria's, page silent.

1802: Ranjit Singh takes Amritsar. 'In 1802, Ranjit Singh, aged 22, took Amritsar from the Bhangi Sikh misl'; the Sikh Empire page calls it the start of 'a decade-long process of conquest of remaining Sikh misls', completed in 1813.

1807: Kasur falls. 'In 1807, forces of Ranjit Singh attacked Kasur and, after a month of fierce fighting, captured it.' The Ranjit Singh page calls it a 'Muslim-ruled principality'; Cliopatria's Sikh Confederacy shape of 1806 is the same land.

1809: the Kangra hill country. The Sikh Empire page lists Kangra and Chamba as a province but dates nothing; the Gorkha army of Amar Singh Thapa went back to the Sutlej 'as per agreement on 24 August 1809' before the Sikh forces (Amar Singh Thapa page, read for the Nepal dossier). Confidence 1: year bridged, page silent on the Sikh entry. Cliopatria adds the land only in 1820.

25 April 1809: the Sutlej becomes the frontier. The Treaty of Amritsar 'demarcated eastern borders of Sikh Empire at Sutlej'; it 'pushed the boundary of British India from the Yamuna to the Sutlej' and Ranjit Singh 'had vacated his control over Faridkot and Ambala' and could not ally with the cis-Sutlej chiefs. Those lands were never inside a Cliopatria Sikh shape; the loss is a caption for the sharp Sutlej line.

region.text: Attock Fort and the Indus crossing

ledger.note: 1813: Attock falls. 'In 1813, Ranjit Singh's general Mohkam Chand led the Sikh forces against the Afghan forces of Shah Mahmud'; 'The Afghans lost their stronghold of Attock Fort in that battle' (the Sikh Empire page: 'the Sikh Empire's first significant victory over the Durrani Empire'). Cliopatria's shape holds Attock only from 1820.

1818: Multan conquered. 'Multan was conquered in 1818, which ended Afghan influence in Punjab.' The Ranjit Singh page: 'In 1818, Darbar's forces led by Kharak Singh and Misr Dewan Chand occupied Multan, killing Nawab Muzaffar Khan'. Cliopatria's shape holds Multan only from 1822.

1819: the Kashmir Valley. 'In 1819, after the battle of Shopian, Ranjit Singh successfully defeated the Afghans and annexed the Kashmir Valley'; the same page has his rule then expanding 'towards the north and the Jhelum Valley'.

ledger.counterpart: Dera Ghazi Khan (Mirani nawabs under Kabul)
ledger.note: 1819: Dera Ghazi Khan. 'The city was taken by the Sikh army of Ranjit Singh in 1819'; 'In the beginning of the 19th century, Zaman Khan was the ruler of Dera Ghazi Khan under Kabul' and 'Fifteen generations of Miranis ruled the area till the 19th century'. The Sikh Empire page puts it in the Multan province.

region.text: Mankera and the Sind Sagar Doab

ledger.note: 1821: Mankera and the Sind Sagar Doab. 'With the defeat of the Nawab of Mankera in 1821, the entire Sind Sagar Doab came under subjugation by the Sikhs.'

1823: Peshawar pays tribute. 'Peshawar became tributary in 1823.' The Ranjit Singh page has the Yusufzai fighting his army in 1823 and Yar Mohammad Khan later reinvested as governor of Peshawar. A lighter tint until the annexation.

region.text: Hazara and the Pothohar fringe, as Cliopatria's 1830 step

ledger.counterpart: Hazara and Pothohar chiefs (page silent on the holder)
ledger.note: 1830: the Hazara and Pothohar fringe. Hari Singh Nalwa 'achieved important victories in Hazara and Peshawar' (no year on the page); Cliopatria adds 5,800 km2 at 72.9-73.5 E, 33.1-34.5 N in 1830. Confidence 1: year Cliopatria's, page silent.
1834: the tribute ends in annexation. 'Peshawar was formally annexed in 1834 by the Sikh Empire.'

1834: Peshawar annexed. 'Peshawar was formally annexed in 1834 by the Sikh Empire.' The Ranjit Singh page has Yar Mohammad Khan 'pardoned and was reinvested as governor of Peshawar with an annual revenue' after Azim Khan's 1834 advance was beaten.

1834: the Dogra conquest of Ladakh begins. 'In 1834, Gulab Singh sent Zorawar Singh to take control of the territory between Jammu and the Tibet border, leading to the conquest of Ladakh and Baltistan'; the Sikh Empire page: 'he sent his general Zorawar Singh to conquer the Namgyal kingdom in 1834' and 'By 1840 Ladakh and Baltistan had been brought under Sikh suzerainty by Gulab Singh'. Control was only 'firm' by 1840, so the year is the start of the conquest.

region.text: Dera Ismail Khan and the Derajat

ledger.counterpart: Sadozai nawabs of Dera Ismail Khan
ledger.note: 1836: Dera Ismail Khan. The city stayed with the Sadozai nawabs 'until it was annexed by Sikh ruler Maharaja Ranjit Singh of the Sikh Empire in 1836'; Diwan Lakhi Mal was made Kardar and the nawabs kept their title and some income.
1839-1840: Baltistan. 'Baltistan, under the rule of Ahmad Shah Maqpon of Skardu, was conquered in 1839-40 by Zorawar Singh, bringing it under suzerainty of the Sikh Empire.'

region.text: western Tibet: Rudok, Gartok, Taklakot up to the Mayum Pass

ledger.note: 1841: the Dogra invasion of western Tibet. In the Sino-Sikh War ('fought from May 1841 to August 1842') Zorawar Singh's force took Rudok and Taklakot and claimed western Tibet up to the Mayum Pass, 'originally called Ngari' on the page's account.

December 1841: the Dogras are beaten in western Tibet. 'Taklakot was retaken on 9 November 1841' and Zorawar Singh was killed at Do-yo ('second day, 11th month' in the Tibetan report, 14 December 1841). The 17 September 1842 treaty kept 'the status quo ante bellum'.

region.text: the Sutlej frontier, from Ferozepur to Ludhiana

ledger.note: 11 December 1845: the Sikh army crosses the Sutlej. the Sikh army began crossing the Sutlej on 11 December 1845 and the British declared war (the page's account); Mudki 18 December, Ferozeshah 21 December 1845, Aliwal 28 January and Sobraon 10 February 1846.
9 March 1846: the First Anglo-Sikh War ends in the Treaty of Lahore (the page dates the war 11 December 1845 to 9 March 1846).

region.text: the Jullundur Doab between the Beas and the Sutlej

ledger.note: 9 March 1846: the Jalandhar Doab goes. the Sikhs had to give up the Jullundur Doab, the region 'between the Beas and Sutlej rivers'; the infobox adds the annexation of 'Lahore's Cis Sutlej territories'.

region.text: Kashmir, Jammu, Hazara and the hill country between the Beas and the Indus

ledger.note: 9 March 1846: Kashmir, Hazara and the hills. Unable to raise the 15 million rupee indemnity, the Lahore Durbar ceded Kashmir, Hazara and the hill territories between the Beas and the Indus to the East India Company, valued at 10 million rupees (the page's account). On 16 March 1846 the Company sold Kashmir 'and its dependencies' to Gulab Singh for 75 lakh rupees (Treaty of Amritsar), and kept the land between the Beas and the Ravi with Kangra and Kullu; Hazara went to Gulab Singh at first.

16 March 1846: Ladakh passes with Gulab Singh. The Treaty of Amritsar gives him 'all the hilly or mountainous country with its dependencies' between the Indus and the Ravi; the page does not name Ladakh. The Dogra rulers of Ladakh become Gulab Singh's own state (kashmir-and-jammu).
16 March 1846: Baltistan passes with Gulab Singh (see the Ladakh entry; the page does not name Baltistan).
Early 1847: Hazara comes back to Lahore. Hazara was initially part of the transfer to Gulab Singh, who in early 1847 'ceded Hazara back to the' Lahore Darbar (the page's account).

region.text: Multan, and the doabs between the Chenab and the Jhelum where Ramnagar (22 November 1848), Chillianwala (13 January 1849) and Gujrat (21 February 1849) were fought

ledger.note: April 1848: the Multan revolt. Patrick Vans Agnew and William Anderson were attacked and murdered at Multan after Mulraj's forces and a city mob turned on them, and the Sikh troops then joined 'open rebellion'; Chattar Singh rebelled in Hazara in August 1848. Under the Treaty of Bhairowal (December 1846) a British Resident held 'full authority to direct and control all matters in every Department of the State'.

12 March 1849: the Sikh army surrenders. Chattar Singh and Sher Singh surrendered to Sir Walter Gilbert near Rawalpindi with about 20,000 men; the Sikh Empire page gives 14 March. Multan fell on 22 January 1849, Gujrat was won on 21 February 1849.

region.text: the whole Lahore state, the Punjab with Multan, Peshawar, Hazara and the Derajat

ledger.note: 29 March 1849: the Sikh Empire ends. 'On 29 March 1849, a durbar was convened at a fort where Eliot read a proclamation on the ending of the Sikh kingdom'; the page also has a proclamation on 30 March and 'Formal annexation occurred on 2 April 1849' (Second Anglo-Sikh War page: Dalhousie proclaimed the annexation on 2 April; infobox 29 March). Duleep Singh signed the confirmation.

wars.name: Afghan-Sikh Wars
wars.outcome: Sikh conquest of Attock (1813), Multan (1818), Kashmir (1819), Peshawar (tributary 1823, annexed 1834); the Battle of Jamrud (1837) was 'the last confrontation with the Afghans at the western boundaries of the Sikh Empire'.
wars.note: Not opened as an article of its own; the dated sentences are those of the Sikh Empire and Ranjit Singh pages. In 1835 the Afghans and Sikhs met at the Khyber Pass 'without a battle'; 'Jamrud formed the westernmost limit of the Sikh Empire'.

wars.name: Sino-Sikh War

zones.text: western Tibet and the Ladakh frontier

wars.outcome: Stalemate: Zorawar Singh took Rudok and Taklakot, was killed at Do-yo in December 1841, and the Dogras won at Chushul in August 1842; the treaty of 17 September 1842 kept the status quo ante bellum and the old frontier between Ladakh and Tibet.
wars.note: The page calls it a war between the Dogra-led Kingdom of Jammu and Tibet; the Sikh Empire's part is its suzerainty over Ladakh and Baltistan.

wars.name: First Anglo-Sikh War
wars.outcome: British victory at Sobraon (10 February 1846); the Treaty of Lahore (9 March 1846) cost the Jullundur Doab, Kashmir, Hazara and the hills between the Beas and the Indus and a 15 million rupee indemnity; the Treaty of Bhyroval (16 December 1846) put a British Resident in charge at Lahore.
wars.note: The Treaty of Amritsar (16 March 1846) then sold Kashmir to Gulab Singh for 75 lakh rupees.

wars.name: Second Anglo-Sikh War
wars.outcome: British victory at Gujrat (21 February 1849); the Sikh army surrendered at Rawalpindi on 12 March 1849; the Punjab was annexed (proclaimed 29 March, formally 2 April 1849).
wars.note: Chillianwala (13 January 1849) is called a strategic British defeat; Multan surrendered on 22 January 1849.

certainty.note: No page opened gives a boundary; the Cliopatria shapes are approximate and the misl frontiers moved with each conquest.

The Sutlej frontier with the Company is sharp from the Treaty of Amritsar of 25 April 1809, which 'demarcated eastern borders of Sikh Empire at Sutlej'; the Afghan frontier (Jamrud, the Khyber) and the Himalayan frontiers with Tibet are approximate.

The Treaties of Lahore (9 March 1846) and Amritsar (16 March 1846) and the 1847 Lahore-Jammu agreement fix the eastern and northern lines (the Beas, the Ravi, the Jhelum and Kishanganga); the western frontier is approximate.

notes: Written by sa-05-f on 2026-10-20 from nine opened Wikipedia pages (the page budget for 15 shapes is 9). (1) LIFE SPAN. Cliopatria's rows run 1799-1848; the dossier ends in March 1849 (proclamation 29 March, formal annexation 2 April), with a new 1849 keyframe, and starts on 7 July 1799. (2) THE 1800 JUMP. Cliopatria draws Lahore alone in 1799 (2,700 km2) and 57,500 km2 in 1800, beside a Sikh Confederacy row (5,600 km2 in 1800-1802, 3,100 km2 in 1803-1806; the other misls). The pages opened date only Jammu (1800), Amritsar (1802), Kasur (1807) and 'all the remaining Sikh misls' by 1813, so the 1800 core is flagged (confidence 1) and the sikh-confederacy dossier (another batch) should settle which lands were Ranjit Singh's in 1800-1813. (3) CORRECTIONS TO CLIOPATRIA. Jammu is missing before 1820. Multan (1818) and Dera Ghazi Khan (1819) are missing from the 1820-1821 shape. The Peshawar valley is inside the shape from 1820 although it was tributary from 1823 and annexed in 1834 (now a vassal tint 1823-1834). Ladakh and Baltistan are drawn as direct land from 1834 and 1840; the pages call them Dogra conquests under Sikh suzerainty (vassal tint to March 1846). The 1836-1845 shapes reach Shikarpur (27.8 N) where the page's southern limit is Mithankot; Sindh is removed. Hazara is missing in 1848 and should not be in 1846. (4) NOT OPENED (page budget). The Misl page, Battle of Shopian, Siege of Multan (1818), Battle of Peshawar (1834), Battle of Jamrud, Kangra Fort, the Treaty of Lahore (1846) and Bhyroval as articles of their own, the Afghan-Sikh Wars article, the Talpur dynasty and the Sikh claim on Shikarpur (1836-1838), Gilgit and the 1842 northern step, the Kohat, Bannu and Derajat dates before 1836, the Pothohar and Hazara step of 1830. A gap-filler should open 'Afghan-Sikh Wars', 'Battle of Peshawar', 'Kangra Fort' and 'Talpur dynasty'. (5) ELSEWHERE. The british-empire (or british-colonial-empire) dossier should record the Treaty of Bhyroval (16 December 1846) as a protectorate over the remaining Lahore state (vassal_start 1846 month 12, vassal_end 1849) and the Punjab gain of 1849; the kashmir-and-jammu dossier should take Kashmir from the British on 16 March 1846 and Hazara back to Lahore in early 1847; the tibet dossier should note the Dogra invasion of 1841. (6) COUNTERPARTS WITHOUT DOSSIERS: sukerchakia-misl, kangra-state (Katoch), the Raja of Jammu (Dogras), Kasur, the Nawabs of Multan, Mankera, Dera Ghazi Khan and Dera Ismail Khan, Peshawar's Afghan governors, the Namgyal kingdom of Ladakh and the Maqpon of Skardu. Region names the gazetteer lacks: Ngari (western Tibet) and Hazara (carried as Cliopatria differences). The native names are the Punjabi and Persian forms in common use, not read from the pages.
